module: C1 Atomic Structure and Periodic Table

Atomic Structure.intro: The atom is the basic unit of all matter. Understanding atomic structure is essential for all of chemistry.

sections.title: Structure of the Atom
points: Nucleus contains protons (+) and neutrons (0)
Electrons (-) orbit the nucleus in shells
Atom is mostly empty space
Proton number (atomic number) = number of protons
Mass number = protons + neutrons
Atoms are neutral: number of protons = number of electrons

sections.title: Isotopes
sections.text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
points: Same chemical properties (same electron configuration)
Different physical properties (different mass)
Examples: Carbon-12 and Carbon-14; Hydrogen and Deuterium

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Relative atomic mass (Ar) = weighted average mass of all isotopes, taking into account their relative abundance.

keyTerms.def: Number of protons in the nucleus — defines the element
Total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Weighted average mass of an element's isotopes

examTips: Atomic number = protons = electrons (in neutral atom)
Isotopes have SAME atomic number, DIFFERENT mass number.
commonMistakes: Saying isotopes have different numbers of protons — they don't, only neutrons differ.
Confusing mass number (p+n) with atomic number (p only).
clozePassages: An atom consists of a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in shells. Protons have a positive charge, neutrons have no charge, and electrons have a negative charge. The number of protons equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom, so the overall charge is zero. The atomic number is the number of protons and identifies the element.

The mass number of an atom is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. For example, carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon atoms but carbon-14 has two extra neutrons. The relative atomic mass takes into account the abundance of each isotope.

Electrons are arranged in shells around the nucleus. The first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons, the second and third shells hold up to 8 electrons each. The arrangement of electrons is called the electronic configuration. The number of electrons in the outer shell determines the chemical properties of the element. Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same number of outer shell electrons.

Ions are atoms or groups of atoms that have gained or lost electrons and have an overall electric charge. A cation is a positively charged ion formed when an atom loses electrons. An anion is a negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains electrons. The charge of an ion depends on how many electrons are gained or lost. Metal atoms tend to form cations; non-metal atoms tend to form anions.

The Periodic Table.intro: The periodic table organises all known elements by their atomic structure. Understanding its layout is fundamental to chemistry.

sections.title: Organisation of the Periodic Table
points: Elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number
Rows = periods (same number of electron shells)
Columns = groups (same number of outer electrons → similar properties)
Metals on left, non-metals on right, metalloids on staircase line
Group number = number of outer electrons (for groups 1-7)

sections.title: History
points: Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass and properties (1869)
Left gaps for undiscovered elements — predictions proved correct
Modern table arranged by atomic NUMBER, not mass
Transition metals form a block in the middle

keyTerms.def: A horizontal row in the periodic table — same number of electron shells
A vertical column — elements with same number of outer electrons, similar properties
Elements in the central block of the periodic table

examTips: Group 1 = 1 outer electron. Group 7 = 7 outer electrons. Group 0 = full outer shell.
Going down a group: same outer electrons, more shells, more reactive (Group 1) or less reactive (Group 7).
commonMistakes: Forgetting Mendeleev used atomic mass, not number.
clozePassages: The periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number. Elements in the same vertical column are in the same group and have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of outer shell electrons. Elements in the same horizontal row are in the same period. The number of electron shells equals the period number. Metals are on the left and non-metals on the right.

Transition metals are found in the central block of the periodic table between groups 2 and 3. They have high melting points, are hard and dense, and are good conductors of heat and electricity. Many transition metals form coloured compounds and can act as catalysts. Iron, copper, and titanium are important transition metals used extensively in construction and engineering.

The properties of elements follow repeating patterns called periodicity. As you go across a period, elements change from metals to non-metals. Going down a group, elements become more reactive (for metals) or less reactive (for non-metals). The atomic radius increases down a group as more electron shells are added. These trends allow scientists to predict the properties of elements based on their position in the periodic table.

Groups.intro: Groups of elements share similar chemical properties because they have the same number of outer electrons. Group 1, 7 and 0 are the most important for GCSE.

sections.title: Group 1 — Alkali Metals
points: 1 outer electron — highly reactive; react vigorously with water
Reactivity INCREASES down the group — outer electron further from nucleus, easier to lose
Reactions with water: metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen
Lithium < Sodium < Potassium < Rubidium (reactivity order)
Stored under oil — react with air and water

sections.title: Group 7 — Halogens
points: 7 outer electrons — need 1 more to complete outer shell
Reactivity DECREASES down the group — outer shell further away, harder to gain electron
More reactive halogen displaces less reactive from solution (displacement reaction)
Fluorine > Chlorine > Bromine > Iodine (reactivity order)

sections.title: Group 0 — Noble Gases
points: Full outer shell — very unreactive (inert)
Exist as single atoms (monatomic)
Used in: light bulbs (argon), balloons (helium), fluorescent lighting (neon, argon)
Boiling point increases down the group

keyTerms.def: Group 1 elements — highly reactive metals with 1 outer electron
Group 7 elements — reactive non-metals with 7 outer electrons
Group 0 elements — unreactive gases with full outer shells
More reactive halogen pushes out less reactive halogen from a compound

examTips: Group 1 reactivity INCREASES down group (outer electron further away → easier to lose).
Group 7 reactivity DECREASES down group (outer shell further → harder to gain electron).
Noble gases are inert because they have full outer electron shells.
commonMistakes: Saying Group 7 reactivity increases down the group — it DECREASES.
Forgetting that Group 1 metals float on water and fizz — they react vigorously.
clozePassages: Group 1 elements are called alkali metals. They are very reactive metals that react vigorously with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost. Lithium, sodium, and potassium are all stored in oil to prevent reaction with air or water.

Group 7 elements are called halogens. They are non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules. Their reactivity decreases down the group. Fluorine is the most reactive, chlorine is a yellow-green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid, and iodine is a grey solid. A more reactive halogen will displace a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt — this is called a displacement reaction.

Group 0 elements are called noble gases. They are extremely unreactive because their outer electron shells are full. They exist as individual atoms and do not form compounds under normal conditions. Helium is used in balloons and airships. Neon is used in advertising signs. Argon is used to provide an inert atmosphere in light bulbs and welding. Their low reactivity makes them very safe to use.

History of the Atom.intro: Our understanding of atomic structure has developed over time as new experimental evidence emerged. This is a great example of how scientific models change.

sections.title: Timeline of Atomic Models
numbered: Thomson (1904) — 'plum pudding' model; electrons embedded in positive sphere
Rutherford (1909) — nuclear model; most mass in tiny positive nucleus; electrons around it (alpha scattering experiment)
Bohr (1913) — electrons in fixed circular orbits (shells) at specific energies
Modern model — electrons in orbitals (probability clouds); subatomic structure of nucleus

sections.title: Rutherford's Alpha Scattering Experiment
points: Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil
Most passed straight through (atom mostly empty space)
Small number deflected at large angles (hit dense positive nucleus)
Very few bounced back (nucleus is very small and very dense)
This disproved the plum pudding model

keyTerms.def: Thomson's model with electrons embedded in a positive sphere
Rutherford's model with a small dense positive nucleus and orbiting electrons
Rutherford's experiment firing alpha particles at gold foil to probe atomic structure

examTips: Describe Rutherford's results AND what they mean: most pass through (mostly empty space); some deflect (small positive nucleus).
Models change when new evidence cannot be explained by the existing model.
commonMistakes: Saying Rutherford's experiment proved the plum pudding model — it DISproved it.
Forgetting that the plum pudding model had a POSITIVE sphere with electrons in it.
clozePassages: Our understanding of atomic structure has developed over time. John Dalton proposed that atoms were solid, indivisible spheres. J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model, where electrons were embedded in a positively charged sphere. Ernest Rutherford carried out the gold foil experiment and discovered the nucleus, replacing the plum pudding model.

Rutherford's gold foil experiment fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most particles passed straight through, but some were deflected at large angles and a few bounced back. This showed the atom was mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre. Niels Bohr later refined the model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels called shells.

The modern model of the atom includes a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons in orbitals at different energy levels. James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, explaining why the mass of atoms was greater than the number of protons suggested. Scientific models are revised as new evidence emerges — the development of the atomic model is a good example of how science progresses through evidence and peer review.
